name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AR_Q01 - Boiling points of aldehydes and ketones

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Aldehydes and ketones have higher boiling points than hydrocarbons and ethers of comparable molecular masses.

Reason (R): Aldehydes and ketones exhibit weak molecular association due to dipole-dipole interactions between their polar carbonyl groups.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The boiling point of a molecular compound depends on the strength of its intermolecular forces of attraction. Stronger intermolecular attractions require more thermal energy to separate the molecules into the vapour phase.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
In aldehydes and ketones, the carbonyl group (\(\mathrm{>C=O}\)) is significantly polarised because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon. In contrast, hydrocarbons are non-polar (only weak van der Waals forces) and ethers have much lower polarity. Therefore, aldehydes and ketones have higher boiling points than hydrocarbons and ethers of comparable molecular masses, making the assertion correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Because of the polarity of the carbonyl group, neighbouring aldehyde or ketone molecules experience dipole-dipole interactions, leading to weak molecular association. Thus, the reason is also correct and directly accounts for the higher boiling points stated in the assertion.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both statements are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.
(A) is incorrect but (R) is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AR_Q02 - Boiling points of carboxylic acids and alcohols

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than alcohols of comparable molecular masses.

Reason (R): Carboxylic acids form hydrogen bonds with water, whereas alcohols do not form intermolecular hydrogen bonds.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Intermolecular hydrogen bonding strongly elevates the boiling points of organic compounds by requiring additional energy to break the hydrogen-bonded network during vaporisation.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Carboxylic acids exhibit more extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding than alcohols of comparable molecular masses; in fact, most carboxylic acids exist as hydrogen-bonded dimers even in the vapour phase. Hence, carboxylic acids boil at higher temperatures than alcohols of similar molar mass, so the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Alcohols also possess an \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group and readily form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with other alcohol molecules as well as with water. Claiming that alcohols do not form intermolecular hydrogen bonds is chemically incorrect. Therefore, the reason is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The assertion is correct, whereas the reason is incorrect.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AR_Q03 - Reactivity of aldehydes versus ketones

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition reactions.

Reason (R): Two alkyl groups in ketones cause greater steric hindrance to the approaching nucleophile and reduce the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon more effectively than one alkyl group in aldehydes.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In nucleophilic addition reactions, a nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon atom of the polar carbonyl group perpendicular to the plane of its \(sp^2\)-hybridised orbitals, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Aldehydes consistently undergo nucleophilic addition faster and more readily than ketones, so the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Two factors govern this reactivity trend: (i) sterically, two relatively bulky alkyl groups in ketones hinder the approach of the nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon more than a single alkyl group and a hydrogen atom in aldehydes; (ii) electronically, two electron-donating alkyl groups reduce the positive partial charge (electrophilicity) on the carbonyl carbon more effectively than one alkyl group. Thus, the reason is correct and directly explains the assertion.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both statements are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AR_Q04 - Reactivity of benzaldehyde compared to propanal

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Benzaldehyde is less reactive than propanal towards nucleophilic addition reactions.

Reason (R): Benzaldehyde undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction on heating with concentrated alkali.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The reactivity of a carbonyl compound towards nucleophilic addition depends on the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon and steric accessibility. Separately, aldehydes lacking an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom undergo disproportionation (Cannizzaro reaction) in concentrated alkali.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
In benzaldehyde, the carbonyl group is conjugated with the benzene ring. Resonance delocalises \(\pi\)-electrons from the aromatic ring onto the carbonyl group, reducing the polarity and electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon compared to propanal. Therefore, benzaldehyde is less reactive than propanal towards nucleophilic addition, making the assertion correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Benzaldehyde does not possess any \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom, so when heated with concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), it undergoes self-oxidation and reduction (Cannizzaro reaction) to form benzyl alcohol and sodium benzoate. Thus, the reason is also a correct statement, but it describes a different reaction and does not explain why benzaldehyde is less reactive than propanal in nucleophilic addition.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both statements are correct, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.
(A) is incorrect but (R) is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AR_Q05 - Fehling test response of aromatic aldehydes

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Aromatic aldehydes give a positive Fehling's test by forming a reddish-brown precipitate of \(\mathrm{Cu_2O}\).

Reason (R): Fehling's reagent is a mild oxidising agent prepared by mixing equal amounts of aqueous copper sulphate and alkaline sodium potassium tartarate.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Fehling's test is a mild oxidation test used to distinguish aliphatic aldehydes from ketones and aromatic aldehydes.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Aliphatic aldehydes are oxidised by Fehling's reagent to carboxylate anions while \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is reduced to a reddish-brown precipitate of \(\mathrm{Cu_2O}\). However, aromatic aldehydes do not respond to Fehling's test. Therefore, the assertion is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Fehling's reagent consists of two solutions mixed in equal amounts before testing: Fehling solution A (aqueous copper sulphate) and Fehling solution B (alkaline sodium potassium tartarate, also known as Rochelle salt). It acts as a mild oxidising agent. Thus, the reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The assertion is incorrect, whereas the reason is correct.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AR_Q06 - Acidity of carboxylic acids versus phenols

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Carboxylic acids are stronger acids than phenols.

Reason (R): The carboxylate ion is stabilised by two equivalent resonance structures in which the negative charge is delocalised over two electronegative oxygen atoms, whereas the phenoxide ion has non-equivalent resonance structures with negative charge on less electronegative carbon atoms.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The acid strength of an organic acid is directly related to the stability of its conjugate base formed upon deprotonation.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Carboxylic acids typically have \(\mathrm{p}K_a\) values around 4–5 (e.g., 4.76 for acetic acid), whereas simple phenols have \(\mathrm{p}K_a\) values around 10. Thus, carboxylic acids are significantly stronger acids than phenols, making the assertion correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
The conjugate base of a carboxylic acid, the carboxylate ion (\(\mathrm{RCOO^-}\)), is stabilised by two equivalent resonance structures in which the negative charge resides entirely on two electronegative oxygen atoms. In contrast, the phenoxide ion has non-equivalent resonance structures in which the negative charge is delocalised onto less electronegative ring carbon atoms, making resonance stabilisation less effective than in the carboxylate ion. Therefore, the reason is correct and directly explains the assertion.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both statements are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AR_Q07 - Electrophilic substitution in aromatic carboxylic acids

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Aromatic carboxylic acids do not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction.

Reason (R): The carboxyl group is an activating and ortho, para-directing group on the benzene ring.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrophilic aromatic substitution on substituted benzenes depends on the electronic nature of the existing substituent and its interaction with the Lewis acid catalyst.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Aromatic carboxylic acids do not undergo Friedel-Crafts alkylation or acylation because the carboxyl group is strongly deactivating and the Lewis acid catalyst, anhydrous aluminium chloride (\(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\)), gets bonded to the carboxyl group. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
The carboxyl group (\(-\mathrm{COOH}\)) withdraws electron density from the benzene ring, acting as a deactivating and meta-directing group during electrophilic substitution (such as nitration or bromination), not an activating or ortho, para-directing group. Thus, the reason is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The assertion is correct, whereas the reason is incorrect.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.
(A) is incorrect but (R) is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AR_Q08 - Conversion of carboxylic acids to acyl chlorides

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Thionyl chloride (\(\mathrm{SOCl_2}\)) is preferred over \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\) and \(\mathrm{PCl_3}\) for converting carboxylic acids into acyl chlorides.

Reason (R): Carboxylic acids having an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom undergo halogenation at the \(\alpha\)-position on treatment with \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) or \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) in the presence of red phosphorus.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The hydroxyl group of a carboxylic acid can be replaced by a chlorine atom using \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\), \(\mathrm{PCl_3}\), or \(\mathrm{SOCl_2}\) to form an acyl chloride. Separately, \(\alpha\)-halogenation of carboxylic acids occurs via the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
In the reaction \(\mathrm{RCOOH + SOCl_2 \rightarrow RCOCl + SO_2 + HCl}\), both side products (\(\mathrm{SO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{HCl}\)) are gases that escape from the reaction mixture, making purification of the acyl chloride much easier than with \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\) or \(\mathrm{PCl_3}\). Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Carboxylic acids containing an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen indeed undergo \(\alpha\)-halogenation with \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) or \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) in the presence of a small amount of red phosphorus (Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction). Therefore, the reason is a correct statement, but it describes an unrelated reaction and does not explain why \(\mathrm{SOCl_2}\) is preferred for acyl chloride synthesis.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both statements are correct, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AR_Q09 - Acidity of unsaturated carboxylic acids

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Direct attachment of a vinyl group to the carboxyl group increases the acidity of the carboxylic acid compared to a saturated alkyl group, contrary to the decrease expected from resonance.

Reason (R): The carboxyl carbon is attached to a more electronegative \(sp^2\)-hybridised carbon atom of the vinyl group, which stabilises the conjugate base.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Substituents directly bonded to the carboxyl group influence acidity through both resonance and inductive effects, where the electronegativity of the hybridised carbon atom plays a decisive role.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Resonance donation from a vinyl (or phenyl) group into the carbonyl group would be expected to decrease acidity. However, experimentally, direct attachment of a vinyl or phenyl group to \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) increases the acidity of the corresponding carboxylic acid compared to saturated aliphatic acids. Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
The carbon atom of the vinyl group bonded to the carboxyl carbon is \(sp^2\)-hybridised, which has greater \(s\)-character and hence higher electronegativity than an \(sp^3\)-hybridised alkyl carbon. This greater electronegativity exerts an electron-withdrawing effect that stabilises the carboxylate anion, thereby increasing acid strength. Therefore, the reason is correct and directly explains the assertion.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both statements are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AR_Q10 - Aldol condensation versus Cannizzaro reaction

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): 2,2-Dimethylbutanal undergoes aldol condensation when treated with dilute alkali.

Reason (R): Aldehydes and ketones having at least one \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom undergo aldol reaction in the presence of dilute alkali due to the acidic nature of \(\alpha\)-hydrogens.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aldol reaction requires the presence of at least one acidic \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom adjacent to the carbonyl group so that a base can abstract it to form a resonance-stabilised enolate ion.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
The structure of 2,2-dimethylbutanal is \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2C(CH_3)_2CHO}\). The \(\alpha\)-carbon (C-2) is bonded to one ethyl group, two methyl groups, and the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group, so it carries zero \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atoms. Consequently, 2,2-dimethylbutanal cannot undergo aldol condensation; instead, it undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated alkali. Thus, the assertion is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Aldehydes and ketones possessing at least one \(\alpha\)-hydrogen undergo aldol reaction in the presence of dilute alkali because of the acidity of \(\alpha\)-hydrogens arising from the electron-withdrawing effect of the carbonyl group and resonance stabilisation of the conjugate base. Therefore, the reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The assertion is incorrect, whereas the reason is correct.

Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AR_Q11 - Base catalysis in cyanohydrin formation

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The addition of hydrogen cyanide (\(\mathrm{HCN}\)) to aldehydes and ketones is catalysed by a base.

Reason (R): The equilibrium for the addition of sodium hydrogensulphite (\(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\)) lies largely to the right for most aldehydes and to the left for most ketones.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both \(\mathrm{HCN}\) addition and \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\) addition are nucleophilic addition reactions to carbonyl compounds, governed by nucleophile strength and steric factors respectively.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Pure \(\mathrm{HCN}\) reacts very slowly with aldehydes and ketones. Adding a base generates the cyanide ion (\(\mathrm{CN^-}\)), which is a much stronger nucleophile and readily adds to the carbonyl carbon to yield cyanohydrins. Hence, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
When sodium hydrogensulphite adds to carbonyl compounds, the equilibrium lies largely to the right for most aldehydes and to the left for most ketones due to steric hindrance around the carbonyl carbon in ketones. Thus, the reason is also a correct statement, but it pertains to \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\) addition and does not explain why \(\mathrm{HCN}\) addition is base-catalysed.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both statements are correct, but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
